title: The priest who never learned to preach
translation: A man made his son a priest. "Study," he told him. "Learn how cause and effect work, and make a living giving sermons." The son did as he was told and set out to become a preacher. First, he learned to ride. "I don't own a palanquin or a carriage. When someone asks me to lead a service and sends a horse to fetch me, it would be awful to slide about on the saddle and fall off." Next he thought, "After the service they might offer me a drink, and if a priest can't do anything at all, the host will be disappointed." So he learned to sing the popular songs of the day. Little by little he got good at both, and the better he got, the more he wanted to get better, so he kept practising. He never found the time to learn to preach, and then he was old.

It isn't just this priest. Everyone does it. When you're young, you have all kinds of plans for the long years ahead: you'll make something of yourself, do something big, learn a skill, study. You keep them in mind. But you think there's plenty of time, so you take it easy, get caught up in whatever is in front of you, and the months and years go by. You finish nothing, and you get old. You never get really good at anything, and your life doesn't turn out the way you meant it to. You can regret it all you like, but you're too old to start again, and you go downhill like a wheel rolling down a slope.

So think hard about what you want most from your life, and weigh the options against each other. Decide what comes first, give up on the rest, and put everything into that one thing. Even within a single day, even a single hour, lots of things come at you. Do the one that's worth even a little more, drop the others, and hurry with what matters. If you cling to everything and won't let any of it go, you won't get anything done.

It's like a game of go. A good player never wastes a move. He stays ahead of his opponent and gives up small things for big ones. Giving up three stones to gain ten is easy. Giving up ten to gain eleven is hard. You should always go for the side that's ahead, even by one stone. But once you have ten, it hurts to let them go, and it's hard to trade them for something only a little better. You want to keep this and grab that too, and that's how you lose this and don't get that.

Say you live in the city and hurry out to the hills on the east side on some business. You've already arrived. If it then occurs to you that going to the hills on the west side would be worth more, turn round at the gate and go west. But you think, "I've come all this way, I might as well see to this first. No day was set for the other thing, so I'll sort it out after I get back." That's how a moment of laziness turns into a lifetime of it. Be afraid of that.

If you're set on getting one thing done, don't be upset when other things fall apart, and don't be ashamed when people laugh at you. You won't get one great thing done unless you give up everything else for it.

Once, in a room full of people, someone said, "There's a thing about masuho grass and masoho grass. The priest at Watanabe knows the tradition." The priest Tōren was there. It was raining, but when he heard this he said, "Has anyone got a straw raincoat and a hat? Lend them to me. I'm going to see the priest at Watanabe and learn about that grass." "Isn't that a bit much? Wait until the rain stops," someone said. "What a thing to say! Does a man's life wait for the rain to clear? If I die, or he dies, who am I going to ask then?" And he ran out, went there and learned it. So the story goes, and I find it wonderful. You don't see that often.

"Be quick, and you get things done," as it says in the Analects. Tōren had to know about that grass. That's how badly we should want to know about the one thing that really matters: what becomes of us after we die.

literal: A certain person made his child a priest and said, 'Study, know the principle of cause and effect too, and make giving sermons and the like your means of getting through the world', so
following the instruction, in order to become a preacher, he first learned to ride a horse.

'When I, a person who has no palanquin or carriage, am invited to be the leading priest (at a service), and they send a horse or the like to fetch me, it would be wretched to fall off with a peach bottom', he thought.

Next, saying 'When, after a Buddhist service, there is a time when they offer sake and the like, if the priest has no accomplishments at all, the patron will think it dreary', he learned the thing called sōka.
As the two skills gradually reached a (good) level, he wanted to do them still better and devoted himself to them, and meanwhile, with no time to learn preaching, he grew old.
It is not only this priest: people in the world in general have this.
While young, in all sorts of matters, to establish oneself, to accomplish a great path, to acquire a skill, to study: the things one plans for the long future, while keeping them in mind,

one thinks of the world as leisurely and keeps slacking, and when one spends the months and days distracted only by the things right in front of one's eyes, one accomplishes nothing in each matter, and one's body grows old.

In the end one does not become skilled at anything, does not make of oneself what one thought, and though one regrets it, it is not an age that can be taken back, so one declines like a wheel running down a slope.
Therefore, among the things one would mainly wish for in one lifetime, compare well which is best, think out and decide the first thing, give up the others, and strive at one thing.
Even within one day or one hour, among the many things that come, do the thing whose benefit is even a little greater, throw away the others, and hurry with the important matter.
If one holds in one's mind not to give up any of them, not one thing will be accomplished.
For example, it is like a person playing go, who does not waste a single move, gets ahead of the other, throws away the small and goes for the large.
In that, to throw away three stones and go for ten stones is easy.
To throw away ten and go for eleven is hard.
One ought to go to the side that is better even by one, but when it has come to ten, one feels it is a pity, and it is hard to exchange them for stones that are not much better.
With a mind that thinks to not throw away this and to take that too, it is the way to not gain that and also to lose this.

A person living in the capital, even if he has business in the Eastern Hills and has hurried and already arrived, if he realises that going to the Western Hills would be of more benefit, should turn back from the gate and go to the Western Hills.

'Since I have come as far as here, let me first say this matter; since it is a thing with no day fixed, the Western Hills matter I will arrange again after going home': because one thinks so, the slackness of one moment becomes the slackness of a lifetime.
One should fear this.
If one thinks to accomplish one thing without fail, one must not grieve that other things are ruined.
One must not be ashamed of people's ridicule either.
Without exchanging all things for it, one great matter will not be accomplished.
Among a crowd of people, someone said, 'There is a thing called masuho grass and masoho grass.
The holy man of Watanabe knows this matter by transmission', and
the priest Tōren, who was present in that company, heard it, and, while it was raining, (said) 'Is there a straw raincoat and hat? Please lend them to me.
I will go and ask at the place of the holy man of Watanabe to learn about that grass', and
when people said, 'That is too hasty. (Go) after the rain stops',
(he said) 'What an awful thing you say. Does a person's life wait for a break in the rain? If I die, or the holy man passes away, could I ask and hear it?' and
it is told that he ran out, went, and learned it: this I feel to be splendid and rare.
'When one is quick, then there is achievement': so it is in the book called the Analects too.
As he wanted to know about this grass, so one ought to have thought of the cause and condition of the one great matter.

notes.quote: 因果の理をも知り、説経などして世渡るたづきともせよ
notes.text: {因果|いんぐわ}の{理|ことわり}: the Buddhist teaching that good deeds bring good results and bad deeds bad ones, in this life or a later one. {説経|せつきやう}: preaching sermons to lay people, which a good speaker could live on. たづき: 'a means' (of living).
{導師|だうし}: the priest who leads a Buddhist service, for example a memorial service for a family. {請|しやう}ず: 'to invite'. The family would send transport to fetch him.
{桃尻|ももじり}: 'a peach bottom', round at the bottom like a peach, so it won't sit still on a saddle. The word is still in dictionaries for a bad rider.

notes.quote: 檀那すさまじく思ふべし
notes.text: {檀那|だんな}: a lay patron who supports a temple or a priest. The 1925 edition explains it as a shortened form of Sanskrit dānapati, 'master of giving'. Modern {旦那|だんな} 'master, husband' is the same word. すさまじ: 'dreary, disappointing', not modern すさまじい 'terrific'.
{早歌|さうか}: a kind of song with a quick rhythm, popular in the Kamakura period, especially among warriors. The 1925 edition only says it was 'probably a kind of popular song of the time'.

notes.quote: 走りて坂をくだる輪の如くに衰へゆく
notes.text: The wheel running downhill: slow at first, then faster and faster, and impossible to stop. The verb is plain {衰|おとろ}ふ, 'to decline'.

notes.quote: 小をすて大につくが如し
notes.text: 'Give up the small, go for the large'. 捨小就大 is one of the maxims in the Ten Precepts of go, a Chinese list that go players still learn today. In go, each player places stones to surround territory, and stones that are surrounded are lost.
{十|とを}: 'ten', historical spelling for modern とお.

The 1925 edition explains {東山|ひがしやま} and {西山|にしやま} as the hills east and west of Kyoto. Both were full of temples and villas. They are on opposite sides of the city, so turning round means crossing the whole of it.

The 1925 edition opens a quotation mark here and never closes it. The thought runs to {思|おも}ひたため ('I'll arrange it'), and with と{思|おも}ふ{故|ゆゑ}に Kenkō speaks again. The translation closes the quotation at that point.

notes.quote: 一時の懈怠すなはち一生の懈怠となる
notes.text: {懈怠|けだい}: laziness, a Buddhist word for slackness in practice. The two halves of the sentence repeat each other, with only 'moment' changed to 'lifetime'.

notes.quote: ますほの薄まそほの薄
notes.text: {薄|すすき}: Japanese pampas grass, a tall grass with feathery heads. The 1925 edition explains that まそほ means 'reddish', so both names mean 'red-headed grass'; ますほ is just a changed form, but at the time the difference was treated as a secret of poetry. Kenkō takes the story from the Mumyōshō, a book about poetry by Kamo no Chōmei (early thirteenth century).
Watanabe was a place on the river mouth in Settsu, in what is now Osaka, a long way from the capital. The 1925 edition says nothing is known about this priest.
Tōren, a poet-priest of the twelfth century. Little is known about him, but his poems are in the Shikashū and later imperial anthologies, as the 1925 edition notes.

notes.quote: 敏きときは則ち功あり
notes.text: From the Analects of Confucius: 敏則有功, 'if you are quick, you will achieve things'. The phrase is in Books 17 and 20. Then Kenkō turns to Buddhism: {一大事|いちだいじ}の{因縁|いんえん}, 'the one great cause', is from the Lotus Sutra, where it is the one reason why buddhas appear in the world. The 1925 edition explains it here as rebirth in paradise in the next life; modern commentaries often take it more broadly as the question of life and death, or enlightenment. べかりける: 'one ought to have'.
